en: To him by whom the eye was opened for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance with the ointment-stick of knowledge.
Obeisances to that glorious guru,
whose shoulders are like those of a lion, whose cheeks are exceedingly sweet with a gentle smile,
and who possesses various wonderful transformations consisting of a radiant rasa that is difficult to comprehend.
May the unified form of Mādhava with Rādhā— possessing a splendor as delightful as the interior of a full-blown golden lotus— protect you.
(Caitanya-candrāmṛta 13)
The cluster of petals formed by her fingers, crimson and glistening,
is colored with the pollen of saffron dust upon the bud-like breasts of Śrī Rādhā;
it is a mass of filaments consisting of the splendor of her nails, which are like the honey of a devotee’s faith.
May the lotus-feet of the enemy of Pūtanā, whose shanks are like stalks, protect us in the ocean of the nectar of the rasa of devotion. (Ānanda-vṛndāvana-campū 1.2)

I pay homage to those who move about, fearing the net of time that has overwhelmed them, who are like fish caught in the ocean of worldly existence, and who have not yet practiced the river of liberation.
In the early morning, Śrī Gauracandra was awakened by the sounds of the Vedic chants from the families of brāhmaṇas at the house of Śrīvāsa.

O mind, worship Him who is fair as excellent gold, whose limbs are suddenly awakened from sleep by sounds resembling the resonance of the Vedas, who experiences the presence of Rādhā at Hari’s side, and whose body is drenched with the tears born of His eyes.

At the end of the night, awakened by the many cries of terrified flocks of birds and by the charming and even unpleasant verses of parrots and mynas, the two rose from their comfortable sleep along with their friends.

I remember Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, who were thrilled upon seeing one another, displaying the playful charms of their newly arisen passion; who, though filled with apprehension at the sound of the *kakka* and *ī* cries, remained full of longing as they reached their respective beds in their own abodes.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.10)
Then, his maidservants— who were ever devoted to their practice as awakened by the occasion of their respective duties—
perceived that the night had ended and abandoned sleep itself.
Did she herself awaken [him]?
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.4) Rising from the bed for a moment with startled eyes, they...
Observing that the sleep of these two sovereigns of the city was a secret sleep, uninterrupted, the women lay down beside them in silence.
They questioned one another with playful smiles and yawns, as they deliberated upon this nectar of rasa.
By my speech, may [the Lord]— whose chest is licked by the swarms of bees that are His own eyes, which roll about due to long-standing wakefulness and infatuation— be attained. (Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 1.6)
Then, one woman whose mind was captivated by the task of preparing flower garlands and betel rolls suitable for serving at the end of the night said to them:
"The surging [passion] of a pair of youths whose limbs are bound by the God of Love..."
"Endowed with fragrance and accessibility, overflowing with aesthetic rasa— know that [the lotus-like faces of the gopīs] have become like travelers on the path of a net. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.7)
Having sent his own glance into another dwelling,
how does sleep delight him as he embraces his beloved, who is so skilled in exceedingly slender dancing?
Here and there, jewel-lamps were placed,
possessing the luster of full-blown blue lotuses and campaka flowers.
He adorns these two with His own clusters of rays,
which are unobstructed ornaments, garlands, and garments.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.9)
Was that dark cloud, surrounded by steady and flickering bees,
perhaps bathing these women— who were engaged in the ritual of their own worship— with the essences of extreme sweetness?
Delighting [him] from the very beginning with appropriate honors,
such as betel, garlands, and various ointments... (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.15)
Passing those few moments, they spent them being presented with incense made of charcoal, grains, and agallochum, appropriate for the occasion.
At that time, the wind-god Prabhajana rejoiced with delight as he adorned the two queens of the forest grove.
I think that upon awakening, with his limbs slack and weak,
he was utterly unable to move quickly.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.17)
At that very moment, he kissed the trees and creepers that had blossomed, filling the ten directions with the weight of their fragrance spread abroad and drawn into his nostrils.
He caused the swarms of bees to awaken,
which were greatly delighted by his resonant humming tones.
Then Vṛndā, having awakened and looked all around,
quickly dispatched birds to keep watch for her two lords, as she was well-acquainted with the proper time.
Those foremost of the twice-born, who previously remained silent even though their minds were yearning for service,
have now become joyful upon receiving that command from Vṛndā.
The swarm of bees, greedy for nectar, warbled all around the pleasure grove.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.12) Then the swarm of bees...
In a charming bower of blossoming clusters of creepers, where heaps of lotuses were made into a couch, the conch-like throat of the Lord of Rati resounded like an auspicious conch.
Like an auspicious drum of love, she makes her humming sound for Govinda.
The swarm of bees, intoxicated by honey, rose up in exuberant joy to awaken Him. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.15)
The row of cuckoos warbled a high-pitched note, clearly in the fifth interval, like the lute of the Mind-born god.
Repeatedly uttering the sound "kuhū," she assumes the melodic modulations of a lute sweet with passion.
Seated beside her lover who warbles with the intoxication of passion,
the swarm of cuckoos utters its sweet, low-toned song upon the mango tree, their throats made resonant by tasting the clusters of tender buds.
Having driven away the deer-like modesty, steadfastness, virtuous conduct, and shame of the gopīs, he was impatient toward the wolves of their pride.
I suspect that, under the guise of the cooing of pigeons, this king of the hyenas of passion roars. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.18)

Who else besides Kṛṣṇa is capable of lifting up the mountain of Rādhā’s fortitude? And who else besides the blessed daughter of Vṛṣabhānu is fully able to bind this wildly intoxicated elephant that is Kṛṣṇa? Here, she alone is highly esteemed.
Why do the peacocks utter their cries at dawn, awakening those two with sounds consisting of short, long, and protracted notes? (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.19)
Even the cock let out the sound "ku-kūkū-kū" at dawn,
just like a young student reciting the Vedas.
Then, although they were awakened by the warbling of birds,
the two of them remained unaware of each other's waking.
Trembling with fear at the loosening of their tight embrace, they remained with eyes closed in that very state. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.21)
That wise parrot, who understood the gestures of the group,
was like a parrot skilled in the meaning of the *Bhāgavata*,
and was expert in awakening the Lord of the worlds.
Being incomparable as the object of love, he spoke thus:
"Victory to you, O one whose expertise in all amorous dalliance is unsurpassed! (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.28).
O nectar for the eyes of the gopīs who are deeply immersed [in You],
O elephant in the river of love for Your life-dear one,
O You who have flooded the entire multitude of worlds with Your own sweetness!
O Ocean of Rasa, it is not fitting that you should immerse yourself in the pleasure of tasting the lips of a beloved and fail to awaken [to Your own nature]. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛtam 1.29)
When you desired to sport, they were indeed disinterested in sporting;
moreover, this night now cuts away every moment.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.30)
Abandon sleep, loosen your embrace,
O Lord; desiring to depart for Vraja, quickly arise in the morning and display your own cleverness.
Therefore, embrace the state of having secret desires;
victory to you, O delighter of Vraja! (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.31)
O Lord, moonlight to the nectar-ocean of Nanda’s heart;
flower of the merit-creeper of Goṣṭheśvarī!
O friend of Gokula, go home and gladden your own kinsmen. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.32)
Victory to You, O Ocean of Rasa!
Arise, leave Your bed which is like the moon, and [embrace] Her who is favorable with love and has taken refuge at the base of Your arms.
To awaken his beloved, who was exhausted by the weight of passion, the dawn rose with swift speed. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.23) Aruṇa attained his rising.
O Lord of Men, feeling natural compassion for the multitude of young women as you were departing quietly for your dwelling, you then hurried from that place to the banks of the daughter of Kalinda.
Then that auspicious Śārī, possessing subtle intelligence,
spoke just as a Śārī bird speaks when established in a position approved by the gods.
O Jayeśvarī, whose lotus face is thirsting for the beauty and fortune of Your own playful charms, O foremost among the young women! (Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 1.33)
O lotus-faced one,
O friend whose limbs are languid from the exertion of amorous play, you sleep!
O virtuous lady, it is no fault of yours that this eastern quarter has been reddened at the end of the night; rather, behold, it was your own unbearable joy that became manifest.
Like the moon's companion, O beloved of the god of love, you now remain as the object of his affection.
O king of lotuses, intoxicated by drinking honey,
that is indeed improper for you;
therefore, I shall wake you this morning.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛtam 1.34) Kṛṣṇa, too, was sleepless while embraced by his beloved; and she, his beloved, was also sleepless while embraced by him.
Though the dawn had already disturbed them, this couple was unable to rise from the bed, for they were not lacking in passion.
(Govindalīlāmṛta 1.38)
Her hips firmly pressed against Kṛṣṇa’s knees,
her breasts held upon his chest, her face placed upon his mouth,
her arms wound around his neck, and her own arms serving as a pillow for him.
Having attained awakening, he does not stir even slightly from his beloved;
he is expert in the compositions of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes, and his wings are fully blossomed with the bliss born of love for Him.
Dakṣa, who was named after him, spoke while taking refuge in the thickets of the grove,
accompanied by hundreds of parrots he had taught.
(Govindalīlāmṛta 1.41)
The female cakravāka bird fixes one eye on her beloved who has quickly departed in the east, where the rays of dawn have begun to appear, while her other eye remains fixed on him still far away;
overcome by anxiety, the owls dwelling in the hollows of the trees fall into silence.
I suspect, O Kṛṣṇa, that the sun has risen;
abandon your sleep.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.32)
Victory, victory to you, O ocean of virtues!
O bond of life to your beloved!
O sun to the lotus of Vraja!

O Lord, you whose summit is adorned with the jewels of the six arts—why indeed do you remain here at the end of the night? Do you even consider the time; is it not fitting that you seek the bed of the forest bower?
And this peacock too, having kept watch throughout the night, has broken his beautiful cry and lacks the discernment to distinguish the end of time.
O Śiva, O Śiva! Even those impoverished by their intense longing for You meet with sleeplessness; who indeed would abandon the time for their own service?
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.24)
Having acquired knowledge from the mouth of Vṛndā,
she who has made many verses her necklace and is intoxicated by the honey of the abundance of love for Rādhā;
"Striving to dispel her sleep" (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.33):
"Abandon your sleep! Abandon your bed in the forest bower!"
Go to your dwelling, my friend; do not fall into indolence; awaken your lover, yet do not awaken the shame of the world.
For the wise elevate their actions when they are appropriate for the occasion; thus,
seated on the lap of the daughter of Vraja’s Lord, he was free from all fear.
O moon-faced one, why do you lie so deeply asleep at the end of the night? O cluster of intoxicated bees, do not remain further in this bower!
O fair-toothed one, do you not take account of the reproach of your elders, though it is undeserved?
Having reached the lap of the night-lilies, you are now hidden there.
The restless swarm of bees, intoxicated with honey, having reached the end of its time,
departs from this undepressed row of lotuses; for Time alone is the lord of languor, joy, and all else.
Your body, with its exceedingly light earrings and crushed pearl necklace,
is like a mass of *śephālikā* flowers from which the blossoms have fallen.
Although these three were of a single form at that time as they are now, nevertheless, Your body was filled with splendors [then]. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.10)
Like a pearl necklace whose beads have fallen and been scattered,
this host of stars of yours is separated from you; and seeing your long sleep, Arundhatī remains dejected, with only a very small portion remaining.
"Look at the circle of the Seven Sages, as if it were your own curved neck," said the śārikās and śukas with their sweet voices (*kala-vacanānām*). (From *Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī* 1.11).
Hearing that voice, exceedingly beautiful and a delight to the ears, Rādhā— who had been disturbed from her sleep—
awoke first; then Kṛṣṇa, who was never satiated by the play of slumber, likewise arose.
The seal [of her composure] is simultaneously shattered by the breaking of both sleeps,
and the play of the corners of both eyes is wondrously manifold.
Filled with the affliction born from the simultaneous whirling of both [eyes],
you have attained sorrow due to the absence of the vision of either [of them].
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.29)
With her anklets jingling melodiously,
she moves with such speed that the splendor of her pair of limbs rises up,
while the tips of her disheveled locks lift as they coil around her.
Their faces were illuminated by the luster of the necklaces on their shoulders,
arising from the flurry of searching for their slipping garments. (Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 1.36)
He perceived him as if he were the very Fortune of the Three Worlds, rising from his couch, charming with his lotus-like hands placed here and there, and full of playful dalliance.
(53) That pair of Rasikas, their eyes rolling and languid, all their limbs relaxed, and their hair disheveled; (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛtam 1.37)
As they stumbled, they somehow managed to support one another by sitting down with their bodies bent over.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.38)
Raising her two arms with their bud-like fingers intertwined,
she performs a graceful stretching of her limbs preceded by a yawn; with eyes closing and her face distressed by the widening of nail-marks upon her breasts.
Thinking again, "No, no," she placed her hand upon Kṛṣṇa’s palm with the intent of scratching it with her nails;
then,
for the sake of concealment, she covered it with her thin garment, which was slipping down from her teeth.

Bathed by the moonbeams, with her lotus-face drawn toward her right hand and her neck gracefully uplifted, Śrī Rādhikā yawned with soft, sweet sounds from the snapping of her left fingers, accompanied by the tinkling of her moving bracelets.
(Alaṅkāra-kaustubhaḥ 5.237) This [hand], turned languidly upward and coiled near the crown of the head,
has its fingers interlocked with one another.
Her pair of arms, joined by the graceful movements of her three-fold bend, shines like the halo around her moon-like face. (Alaṅkāra-kaustubhaḥ 5.238)
Then the Lord, having risen, sat upon the couch;
feigning sleep with eyes closed,
he drew his weary beloved into his lap with both arms.
Beholding her sweetness, the khajarī bird, its eyes rolling, cries out "sādhurīti" (how excellent!). (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.51)
That Acyuta drank in with his eyes the face of his beloved, which resembled a lotus at dawn, with its mass of curling locks like a swarm of bees and its slight smile.
With her pair of arms and all her fingers interlaced,
she was massaging his body while rubbing it thoroughly.
Beholding his beloved with the luster of her teeth revealed by a yawn, Mukunda rejoiced.
(Govindalīlāmṛta 1.53)
At that very moment, did he not illuminate the beauty of her eyes— now blossoming and sleepless— with the ruby-lamps of the rays from her teeth produced by a yawn?
Tasting one another as they lick each other,
[they behold] her who sleeps supine upon his own lap at dawn, her face slightly smiling amidst feigned weeping.
Seeing that beloved, who had her hair half-loosened at the ends, who wore a crushed floral garland, whose necklace was broken, and who—
repeatedly opening her pair of eyes languid with dizziness— was longing to look upon her own face,
the Moon of Vraja attained incomparable joy as she lay exhausted from amorous play.

(From *Govinda-līlāmṛta* 1.54) She whose limbs were like golden lotuses, who was rendered languid by the exhaustion of intense amorous play, her body resting in the lap of her beloved, whose splendor was as lovely as a glossy peacock’s tail—
If the *śampāka* tree had remained steady during the fresh rain-clouds,
it would clearly have attained a state of equality with Śrī Rādhā here.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.55)

The face of Hari, with its shimmering shark-shaped earrings, the arising of a sweet and gentle smile, eyes languid with passion, the fragrance of a lotus, and swaying locks of hair; its lips darkened by the collyrium rubbed away by his own teeth.
Having observed him, the lotus-eyed one again became eager for amorous play,
her modesty born from their mutual gazing. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.56)
Beholding the face of his beloved— with her trembling, half-closed eyes and a slight smile—
Kṛṣṇa’s thirst for her was kindled once again.
With his left hand he raised her head from below,
and with his other hand he held her chin.
With his neck slightly bent, he repeatedly kissed the face of his beloved, whose cheeks were radiant with a smile.
(Govindalīlāmṛta 1.58)
Immersed in an ocean of bliss from the touch of her beloved’s lip, shaking her hand, her eyes slightly squinted,
and her throat faltering with soft syllables of "No, no!"— she spoke.
He spread joy among the eyes of his friends;
His nectar-like form is unique throughout the three worlds.
And this youth of boundless sweetness has attained fulfillment this very day, since her beloved now enjoys it with supreme joy in every way.
Having reflected thus for a moment, she whose entire sweetness was drunk in by his eyes spoke to her beloved.
The lotus of his face, the abode for the play of the beauty of his side-glances shining with extreme joy within his heart.
(Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 2.21)
O you voluptuary,
listen! Since dawn has not yet arrived and my attendants have not followed me, I have been left by you with my garments and ornaments disarrayed.
Why then do you not quickly desire to attain that?
Accomplish your own cleverness and grace me with favor.
Propitiate the bodiless god who is our cherished deity, for he, who dwells within the temple of our hearts,
has been driven out by you by means of these very ornaments.
(From *Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta* 2.23) You speak the truth, O dear one, regarding my beloved deity born from your own body, who has manifested upon the seat of your limbs.
"I worship her with ornaments, garments, perfumes, flowers, garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth"— thus he spoke to her (*Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta* 2.24).
Having thus heard the words of the Queen, she, who was skilled in service,
[prepared] the articles necessary for that purpose.
Eager to offer herself,
she slightly loosened the door that was not yet quite ajar, moving slowly with a gracefulness born of her particular manner of placing her feet.
Having thus resolved, that host of maidservants, free from doubt, entered the chamber for the sake of keeping watch over her (*Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta* 1.26).
These two, with their clusters of rays, render the scattered jewel-lamps here and there as radiant as full-blown blue lotuses and campaka flowers.
Adorned with unobstructed ornaments, garlands, and garments,
their lips were bitten by each other's teeth as they moved languidly in amorous play.

Beholding their two beloveds before them— whose bodies were marked by nail-scratches, whose beauty of leaf-patterned paintings had faded, whose garments and hair were disheveled, and whose pearl necklaces and flower garlands were scattered— they rejoiced again and again.
Then, as he slowly and gently drew the comb held in Bhānumatī’s hand, (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.63).
Her braid of hair was being fashioned into a garland of *mālatī* flowers by one skilled in the art of arranging such tresses.
(Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 2.25)
With well-prepared mixtures of musk, sandalwood, and saffron, he decorated her with a streak of red lac, making her beautiful and variegated like a garland.
He, variegated and charming, holding a fresh wick [of light], [is joined] by those two with a pair of arms to a cluster of cloves.
With beautiful, unprecedented luster produced by fresh collyrium, he adorned her ears; he then anointed those two eyes of hers, which resembled lotuses.
When He wore a necklace entwined with clusters of radiant flowers, His beloved, intoxicated with passion, spoke to Him thus: (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛtam 2.27)
Why do you not seek to repair that sandalwood bodice which was torn by you from your breasts?
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.28)

Today, I shall cause amazement among those various friends of yours, such as Viśākhā and others, who possess excessive pride in their skill in the art of painting, by means of [the marks] made upon their two breasts.
"By means of various and diverse [means]," he said to her (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.29), being intent on demonstrating the purpose of her adornment.
While Hari was marking her two breasts with a stylus, Śrī Rūpa Līlā-rati-mañjarī became the target of his five arrows.
And his hand trembled as he repeatedly wiped away the wondrous tilaka-mark from his forehead with his chest. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.30)
I think that the clever Cupid, desiring to burn her fuel of fortitude, fanned the fire of his passion for her. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.31)
Kāma, having immediately fashioned for him a residence of no small splendor in an unrestricted location,
then wiped it away, joined it together, and shattered it into pieces.
With that very joy, He adorned both of them;
and those maidservants [attained] the fulfillment of their purpose through their blossoming eyes. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.32)
Desiring her for a long time as if she were incarnate,
and wishing to sport with her once more, the two of them met; then, under some pretext, they all went out together.
Again,
through the union of their two beautiful faces which were deeply turned toward one another,
those two beloved ones shone as they entwined each other with their steady, vine-like arms.
Thinking, "May we attain auspiciousness even for a moment through a light sleep," the two of them lay upon that bed of crooked flowers with their limbs relaxed.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.41)
At dawn, those two birds were unable to depart, for their bed was distressed by her separation, and sleep— having somehow managed a slight embrace— was likewise unable to leave.
Even that [pleasure] they performed with these two [lovers], crying out in union;
O you who disregard family discipline, do not lie down in the forest grove!

Abandon this sleep that destroys pleasure; arise quickly! The night has become especially advanced; see, only a fraction of the darkness remains. Do not cause distress to your circle of kinsmen by failing to rise.
O Goddess, behold this eastern quarter that has been born; it bears a stream of deepening crimson hue that imitates your lotus feet.
And this poor, distressed female ruddy goose,
whose union with her mate has been shattered by the onset of the day,
[cries out]— (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.5).

Furthermore, desiring to attain the beauty of your face, this moon— out of excessive greed and disregarding his own desire— has reached the peak of the western mountain, wishing to cast away his own body; look at how lofty it is!
The moon is setting; who could stop it today, O fair-faced one? Cast off your sleep and release the seal of your eyes.
Perceive these women whose faces possess the luster of flashing lightning, who have cast off their ornaments in the heat of passion, whose garments are disarrayed and overturned,
and whose bodies are disheveled; let them all come together and attend upon you.
"O moon-faced one, look! This very deer, nurtured by her own hands, has entered into your presence—she who possesses such graceful limbs. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.9)
O compassionate one, let your sidelong glance, with its slightly arched waves, be cast toward me;
alas, may it be effective for your own pleasure so that I may achieve my purpose.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.12)
O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, your friend, approaching in haste with the thought that your reddish lotus-feet are fresh sprouts— due to her innate purity of heart— bears the longing of your other companions.
O moon-faced one, she who once dealt blows with her lotus-like hand as you departed is now playful in the enjoyment of merely the remains of your food.
Though our sole attention is fixed on the joy of drinking from the nectar of your lotus feet,
we are stricken with grief born from the absence of your glance, and thus we rely solely upon the light of the orb of your moon-like face.
Hari,
filled with great curiosity, measures your pair of eyes, having measured the measureless love within them.
Comparing him with some indescribable string of pure pearls, he of the beautiful countenance surely dispels all doubt.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.15)
When the affectionate śārikās had thus spoken these words, which were pleasant in both sound and meaning, for the purpose of rousing him, the birds, having paused for a moment, bowed down to him.
Having approached the groves and attained a mass of joy,
she then awakened Kṛṣṇa, who was longing for his bed. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.16)
Even the flock of parrots, eager for the joy of Kṛṣṇa,
[delighted him] with their abundant warbling, which was like fine wine— sweet and profound, charming in both sound and meaning, gentle, and a source of pleasure to the ear.
Deep with the essence of affection, firm in their mastery of beautiful words and meanings,
possessing throats sweet with melodious tones, they are unimpeded in their loving conversations.

When there was an opportunity for solitude, some indeed awakened [to their duty], yet alas, they were not truly wise, being utterly bewildered at the time when action was required. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.18)
O fortunate one, at the end of the night, when only a small portion of sleep remained in your bedchamber, your mother shook off her own doubt and,
knowing the time had come, hurried to wake you.
"She has come here of her own accord; affection alone is the counselor in this matter.
You are the knower of the proper time and the sole destroyer of all suffering."

You are the kinsman of the world, an ocean of the multitude of excellent virtues, a vine-like bower and couch, and an embodied personification of joy; yet even so, abandon that [world], for may there be well-being for you through this upward ascent.
The young bees, intoxicated and having reached the end of the harmful season,
have gone to sleep within the forest groves from which the flowers have fallen.
When the distinction of the proper time has arrived, who in this world would not be deluded as they engage in play for a few moments upon the path of lotuses?
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.20)
In one place there is dejection on the face, elsewhere the serenity of a smile; in one place the separation from a beloved, elsewhere union with a lover—
such is the extreme and undeniable disparity between the rows of night-lotuses and day-lotuses.
Does not time become vast with the beauty of agitation? Victory to you, O fortunate one!
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.21) Victory, O Subhaga!
Salutations to you; let it be heard: this copper-crested cock, heavy with the joy of the appointed time for his own service having arrived, is distressed by your long sleep.
For one who is skilled in the conventions [of worldly conduct] is not bewildered at the time of action; thus, having awakened and shaken off his wings...
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.27).
Now, having indeed awakened and shaken off his wings...
Raising their necks, the five or six roosters crowed loudly; at that moment,
Rādhā woke up, her distress relieved.
Thinking that they were specifically obstructing her embrace with Kṛṣṇa’s body,
she cursed them in anger.
Depart quickly, depart from here, O enemies! Why do you, whose weapons are your feet, still cry out there in that very city?
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.21)
Having slightly loosened her embrace from her lover’s chest and perceiving that they had remained silent, she immediately drew him close again with a faint smile and a semblance of sleep.
Furthermore, when cultivated, she triumphs again;
for the eye-fish is caught from the net, and she is its abode. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.22)
The forest of their loveliness intensely cherished even those who purchase a mere spark from the radiance of their joy with tens of millions of the highest sums of wealth.
(From *Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta* 2.1) Viśākhā said to her friend with a playful gesture: "O friend, these two lovely ones are naked, yet they are as beautiful as a heap of fine garments."
Though dwelling in tranquility, they are exceedingly captivating; with their own limbs, which are themselves non-limbs, they are languid yet radiant.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.2)
Due to the playfulness of passion, they were without armlets; alas, being without collyrium, they were mutually unanointed, yet clearly recognizable by the fading redness of their lips.
"Characterized by the state of being the lower lip of the dispeller of [worldly] attachment" (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.3);
then Lalitā spoke: "Let it be understood."
In the battle of love, which of the two emerged victorious—
those two whose lips were bitten, whose heads were tossed by the grasping of hair, and whose chests were wounded by fingernails?
Under the guise of the saffron from her breasts, Rādhā placed her heart’s devotion upon the lotus feet of Acyuta.
Until his eyes, reddened by the sound of the rāva, placed that brilliant [garland] upon his head at her very feet. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.5)
Thus, for a moment, with their limbs unobserved,
they described [the matter] in low voices, greatly extolling their own good fortune.
They have drowned in the great ocean of bliss (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.6);
thereafter, furthermore, those elephants and others—
Shaking off her weariness, she spoke to those who were groaning:
"O friends, forgive me; grant me a moment to lie down. Then she slightly relaxed her limbs.
The kādamba, kāraṇḍava, haṃsa, and sārasa ducks; the pigeons, śārī birds, parrots, peacocks, and cuckoos; (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.23)
Moving through the waters and grounds of the pleasure grove, they sang sweetly of Kṛṣṇa, which is like the nectar of His stories. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 1.24)
Just as a couple, upon waking, simultaneously perceive the pain born of separation and the trembling of their limbs, so too did the sun and moon,
possessing the luster of a campaka flower and a blue lotus and the splendor of a rainbow, respectively.
And through a close embrace, there was joy in their chests; then her companions, their faces smiling with delight—

Laughing among themselves and playfully nudging that friend, they entered the bower— which resounded with the hum of swarms of bees— from all sides, filled with apprehension due to the long-drawn dawn.
Having noticed her friends approaching nearby with smiling faces and flickering eyes, (she became bashful).
Bestowing double the joy upon her beloved, she rose up from the pair of her lover’s thighs. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.61)
Rising in haste, Rādhā covered her body with her yellow upper garment, which she had grasped in her agitation, and sat down by her beloved's side.
Looking at their faces with bashfulness, she,
being deeply attached, was filled with joyful approval.
The very same cluster of beauty belonging to those two lovers sporting in dalliance flourished with joy; it was itself most skillful at enhancing their immediate loveliness.
One placed a pillow behind them,
while another laid soft cloth over the two of them.
By applying nectar-like [words] to his mouth, she dispelled his extreme dizziness and caused his eyes to blossom open. (Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 2.9)

A certain woman, with her garment slightly moistened by flower-water, wiped away the displaced red lac, collyrium, and other pigments from their eyes for the sake of making them appear fresh at every moment.
Did he place a betel-roll in the other [face] to bring his two faces to the state of a mirror? (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.16)

One woman, with her mind fixed on that auspicious *ārātrika* rite, quickly performed it by waving the jewel-lamp wicks before him, as if she were personally performing the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) with millions of her own eyes.
In the center [is the form] smeared with the thick saffron paste from Acyuta’s body, its two flanks variegated by the lac-dye from Rādhā’s feet.
The bed, variegated with spots of vermilion, sandalwood paste, and collyrium, bestows upon them various kinds of amorous play. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.64)
Her arrangement of gathered flowers was slightly crushed;
her limbs were adorned with the dye of betel and collyrium;
and the marks of her lover’s amorous play were becoming clearly visible.
Not seeing his bed, like a child not seeing its own companion,
[he saw] in one place a smear of saffron paste and in another a mark made of vermilion.

On one side, he has as his allies the blood flowing from the wounds inflicted by the enemy of separation; on the other, he possesses the splendor of a bow broken by a garland of flowers. On one hand, his necklace is disarrayed; on the other, the manner of his bowstring is severed.
In some places marked with musk, in others marked with collyrium,
they shine like the fragments of the tusks of the elephant of King Smara.
For he became a theater for the play of love for the lovely-faced friends who had arrived, where waves of curiosity surged forth.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.39)
Showing his own chest to them with a glance, Hari spoke to them,
desiring to behold the faces of his beloveds.
Seeing her beloved about to depart for the moon, which possesses the sweetness of a mixture of emotions,
the female cranes at dawn became fearful of separation.
As if out of a desire to behold the paintings upon the canvas of the sky,
she drew a hundred crescent moons of Rādhā.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.67–68) (128)
While Kṛṣṇa was speaking thus, seeing her friends with their faces smiling, she contracted her tremulous eyes,
her spotless cheeks blossomed, and her eyebrows were tossed and arched.
She gazed at her beloved with crooked side-long glances as if striking him, her eyes half-closed in playful affection and their corners reddened and thick with tears. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.69)
Trembling with modesty and apprehension, smiling with a weight of jealous anger, her pupils dilated as she gazed upon the face of her beloved,
Rādhā’s glance brought immense joy to the eyes of her lover.
Thus, for those two who were immersed in an ocean of the bliss of mutual love,
[I shall describe] the sweetness of their amorous play at dawn.
Having drunk [of that nectar], O friends, those women intoxicated by passion then forgot the conduct appropriate for the present moment. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.71)
Beholding those two immersed in the nectar-ocean of pastimes, as well as their friends blinded by the intoxication of love,
Vṛndā became apprehensive at the rising of her own splendor.
She directed Sārī, who understood her own gestures, [saying]:
"Out of great shame and fear of my husband... (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.72).
The parrot named Śubhā, who wards off the world’s laughter and brings about Rādhikā’s awakening, spoke.
"Your husband will now return from the cowherd settlement having brought loads of milk;
arise, arise, O Rādhā! Perform here in this house the auspicious worship of the site."
"O lotus-eyed friend, go quietly from the thicket to the bedchamber while your husband’s mother has not yet risen from her bed and speaks."

Her heart mired in the mud of suspicion, her husband fears for her; her mother-in-law is anxious, and her husband Abhimanyu— whose name is truly significant— is exceedingly cruel in his pursuit of faults.
Though she is constantly angry and even that dull-witted Nanandā reviles her,
O Kṛṣṇa, you still do not abandon this simple girl who was born at dawn.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.77)
This milk-ocean of her heart, agitated by the falling of the Mandara mountain of Sārī’s words,
now whirls with her eyes as its newly born fish.
Distraught by separation, she rose from her bed;
Kṛṣṇa too [perceived] the beloved state of Vṛṣabhānu’s daughter.
Seeing her face with eyes trembling with fear,
he quickly rose from his own bed, seizing his beloved’s dark blue, fine silk garment.
Then,
having exchanged their garments, the two of them became suspicious of one another.
Supporting one another by the hand,
they emerged from the bower.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.80)
Bearing Rādhā’s hand in His left and the flute in His right, Kṛṣṇa shone as He emerged from the forest groves.
Like a cloud embraced by a garland of lightning,
one [goddess] holds a golden pitcher, while another holds a golden-handled fan.

One friend carried a beautiful mirror; another, a vessel for saffron and sandalwood paste; another, a variegated betel-box inlaid with jewels; and another, a sarika bird in its cage—thus did several friends, their hearts full of joy, emerge from the cottage in the grove.
Another [palanquin] has a cover of sapphire, is adorned with gold, made of ivory, and possesses a casket of vermilion. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.82)
Taking him from the bower like a jasmine bud from the womb of a pregnant woman, she departed with a gentle smile.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.83)

A certain woman, having joyfully gathered from her necklace a cluster of shimmering pearls that had fallen away from the string snapped by an embrace, tucked them firmly into the hem of her own garment.
Binding him, she emerged from the bower-house;
he, who had slipped from her lap during their play.
Quickly taking it from the bed,
Rati-mañjarī went out and placed it at the ear of her mistress.
Taking her bodice from the edge of the bed,
Rūpamañjarī—
The dear joking companion, having gone out, secretly gave [it] to her friend.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.86)
Taking up the spittoon,
the maidservant Guṇamañjarī gave them chewed betel.
Mañjulālī went outside, separating herself from the limbs of those two. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.87)
Taking the withered garlands and ointments from the bed,
she gave them to all [the women] and went out.
Seeing before her her beloved, whose body was shrouded by clouds and sky, and that joyful friend whose limbs were enveloped in yellow garments— (Govinda-līlāmṛtam 1.88).
Laughing, those friends, covering their faces with their hands, gazing at one another with sidelong, tremulous glances, sent them forth in every direction and rejoiced. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.89)
Observing their playful gestures, with blossoming eyes fixed upon each other's faces,
they were submerged in an overflowing ocean of the bliss of love.
They appeared like two figures depicted in a painting;
a garment dark as a rain-cloud clung to the body of the Beloved.
In the thick darkness, Kṛṣṇa was unable to distinguish his beloved,
nor could she recognize her own swelling form; even Hari did not perceive the yellow silk garment clinging to his lover’s body, which was as radiant as gold— like water within a conch shell.
(From *Govinda-līlāmṛta* 1.91) [The river] was agitated by indignation at any obstacle to their drinking of the nectar of those two's pastimes.
They revile the rising dawn;
then Lalitā said to her friend: (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.92)
O Rādhā, look at this dawn;
though his pair of feet has slipped away due to the painful wounds from the playful scratches of his lover, this reddish sun still does not abandon them even now.
"The word *dhruvam* [means] that one's own nature is difficult to abandon" (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.93).
Then, she placed [the sun] in the sky, as red as the dawn.
Her face brightened with a smile born of playful jesting, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu spoke softly and sweetly to Him whose eyes were reddened by anger over the interruption of their amorous play.
Anūru too, having traversed the sky in half a moment as he sets, rises again;
had that Creator made him long-legged, he would have taken even longer.
Even news of the night would not have reached him then,
as he beheld the enchanting splendor of the dawn.
Having drunk in the nectar of her words, Mukunda, his mind uplifted with joy and forgetting the journey to the cowherd settlement, spoke to that mistress of his life.
Beholding him arrived at dawn,

O madwoman, this eastern quarter has become as if reddened by jealousy;
for even the Lord of the Twice-born, the destroyer of the mass of darkness for all people, has become tranquil.
"O beloved, having partaken of wine, you have suddenly fallen upon her from all sides";
thus thinking, the night-lily, ashamed at the sight of the lotus smiling with joy at its union with the sun, I suspect covers her face at dawn with her own contracting petals.
Having seen the disappearance of the darkness at dawn, these cuckoos,
who resemble a mass of darkness at night, are startled in the morning by the moon.
Because she moves through darkness by taking refuge in that friend [the moon], they call her "Kuhū" with their own voices, as if she were swallowed by the new moon.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.99)
Overwhelmed by a weight of bliss born from union with her beloved of spring,
the female dove, under the pretext of cooing, [cried out].
As if sighing in intoxication,
look, the restless bee follows her. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.100)
O moon-faced one, the bee, tawny from sporting with the clusters of night-lotuses, has spent the night in union within the bud of a day-lotus.
Having suspected that her beloved was approaching, she broke her bow. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.101)
Overwhelmed with joy, the female ruddy goose kisses the male ruddy goose with her beak at the Kokanada lake, which is twice as red as the rays of the sun.
O sweet-voiced one, the swan known as Kalasvana,
seeing us, has his wings fully expanded with joy.
Even though he desired to sport, having released the female swan, he goes before you; do not strike him.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.103)
Behold the female cuckoo, her voice sweet with passion, holding in her beak a lotus stalk released by her companion and enjoyed by her mate;
she follows after her lover with her eyes fixed upon your lotus-like face.
Named Tuṇḍiketi, she with the lotus-face is like a female swan;
she dwells upon the peaks of the Malaya mountains and carries the fragrance of lotuses.

The breeze, sporting in the water, bears away the clusters of sweat from the excellent women of that lover; it is capable of teaching the dance of the young maiden-like creepers and dispels all fatigue.
Thus, having observed that [state] of the two Lords, who were engaged in the playful sport of most sweet speech and had forgotten their departure for their own abode—
And those friends, radiant with smiles and intoxicated with joy, were filled with longing for the Queen of the Forest out of fear of the day's end. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.106)
The beloveds arose with their moon-like faces blooming;
the night had passed away, its moonlight and playful charm dispelled—how could there not be a shattering of that splendor? Or rather, let it be as it may.
She reflected in her heart for a moment:
"Just as darkness perishes on all sides... (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.56).
Then, as that light increased more and more, she experienced only pain in her heart;
even the Vedas do not know the nature of Vraja.
Then Vṛndā, who understood his gestures, knew the proper time, and was situated upon a tree— (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.57)
The aged monkey Kakkha illuminated the path (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.107).
Clad in crimson garments, worthy of worship by the virtuous, the ascetic Dawn with the rays of the sun rising upward.
Having heard from them that she was called "Jaṭilā" because of her matted hair, [he said]: "This Jaṭilā has arrived. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.108) Thus, by means of their description of her matted hair—
The three Vedas immediately assumed a pallid hue,
while the very ocean of their splendor was swallowed up by the rising conch-shell.
On the path, fearing those of malicious intent, they cast sidelong glances from their heavy-lidded eyes, which trembled like startled ripples.
May Rādhikā and Kṛṣṇacandra— profoundly endowed with supreme virtues, steadfast in the battle against desire, and tireless in their mutual delight— be victorious. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 1.42)
Neither on the road, nor in the palace, nor in the forest were they noticed,
as they brought festivals for the eyes of their attendants through their innate and constant devotion and their own power of bliss.
Then, as they wandered along the path, those two who are beloved by the world shone forth,
lifting up their slipping silken garments, their locks of hair, and their flower garlands.
Seeing those two departing separately along the dense path, trembling with fear, her friends named Jaṭilā went hither and thither in all directions, agitated with alarm.
To his left were the attendants of Candrāvalī and the elders of the cowherd village;
in front was Kṛṣṇa, and behind him was Kuilajāṭilā, whom he perceived as having arrived.
Eager to see his beloved as she walked away with fearful and hurried steps,
he came to the cow-pen, turning his neck and casting his eyes in every direction.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.111)
Behold him before you— his garland withered, his lips stained with soot from broken strings of jewels,
his limbs covered in nail-marks, his lotus-eyes rolling—
he stands like a withered stalk, clearly unrecognizable to the cowherd assemblies.
In the cow-pen, as the night was approaching its end, the son of the Lord of the Cowherds entered,
followed by one who suspected him to be a matted-haired ascetic.
Bewildered by the weight of her heavy hips and breasts,
the mistress who held her garment and hair in her hands walked gracefully toward Vraja with a gait that was both swift and lingering.
She does not fear even a serpent as much as she fears a post standing before her;
nor is she agitated by the trumpeting of an elephant as much as by the cawing of a flock of crows.
This [mind] does not become even more deluded in the darkness than it is in the light;
therefore, I think that even in separation, it is not as distressed as it is in the union with its beloved.
(Jagannātha-vallabha-nāṭaka 5.34)
For Rūpamañjarī, having indeed cast aside her own desire— which was veiled by a screen of flickering glances smoky with a mixture of fear and passion— placed it [within him].
Desiring to lead her home, he followed her on the path,
[fleeing] from the swift arrows of her restless glances cast here and there. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 1.113)
Then Rati-mañjarī, along with her attendants, warded off other people who were like the letter *bha*— preceded by the letter *a*— due to the accumulation of heart-activities corrupted by fear.
Surrounded by them, yet unobserved by the people of Vraja,
she entered her own dwelling and then ascended to her bed.
For, distressed by separation from her beloved, she then spoke openly of the pain in her heart to her friend, with a voice choked with tears.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.80)
Having just now drawn me out from my home, O Lalitā,
you cause me to enter once again that very ocean of the nectar of union with Kṛṣṇa’s body.
"Today your attempt at seduction has been rendered in vain, since he whom you sought to entice has now been seen setting behind the western mountain. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.76)
O friend, does that sun of fierce rays desire to ascend the eastern mountain while the night still remains?
"Has it today become like a flower in the sky? (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.77).
"Fie upon my hearing, fie upon my tongue, and fie upon my sight!"
Those who were afflicted by the fever of a constant, heavy longing did not obtain even a single drop of the nectar of his melodious voice,
sweetness, and beauty to drink.
Previously, yoga indeed taught you the path of detachment;
but now, separation makes you simple-hearted.
The First [Lord] revealed the meaning of this [Veda], which is the nectar of immortality; another [the Second Lord] makes it experienced. Alas! Who indeed is the Kālakūṭa [poison] for the *ukāra*?
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.79)
Thus, being entirely overcome by passion, she was not even able to comprehend her friend's words;
how much less could she perceive the lord of her heart again in a dream?
Then the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu fell asleep upon her bed (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 2.80, second half of the verse).
Regarding a certain woman who was asking another woman who was not going to meet her lover, someone said:
Again and again she raises the dark edge of her bodice over her head;
with a hand slack and weak, she bears a body whose ornaments have fallen away;
holding back her braid from which half the pearls have slipped, she casts her eyes about with languid glances.
"Look from the bower; having entered the house, my friend Rādhikā lies down quietly at the proper time, having finished her abundant amorous play in her own abode. (Stava-mālā, Kuñja-bhaṅga 1)
When Acyuta had fallen asleep, the personified Vedas, who are expert in the display of His divine pastimes and endowed with qualities, returned to their respective abodes,
their movements unobserved, just as they had departed from the Lord.
Thus ends the first compendium, titled "The Compendium of Pastime at Night," within the *Śrī Bhāvanā-sāra-saṅgraha*.
This concludes the *Śrī Śrī Bhāvanā-sāra-saṅgraha*.
Prātar-līlā (1): Seeing her son wounded by the Lord during the morning congregational chanting, Śacī said, "Alas!
My son, how has this body of yours become wounded so early in the morning?"
I worship that Gauracandra— who, thus busied with fondling his own son, repeatedly touched him as he lay upon the bed and woke him—
and who is approached on earth by devotees such as Śrīvāsagupta and others who bow down together with him.

I worship that fair-complexioned Hari, whom one should serve with excellent rice after bathing at dawn while inquiring after his welfare, rubbing [his feet], washing his face with water scented with flowers and other fragrances, and recounting the stories of dreams experienced.
In the Root Sūtra:
Rādhā, bathed and adorned, summoned by her friends from Vraja in the early morning, having prepared the cooking of food in her home, ate only what remained from Kṛṣṇa's meal.

I take refuge in Kṛṣṇa—the Buddha who has obtained the cow and the dwelling, who has finished milking the cow, who is well-bathed and has taken his meal—along with His companions; and then I take refuge in Her and in Him.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.1)

The maidservants, who delighted in following their two desires, adorned their bodies— already bathed and anointed— with the remains of the flowers, garlands, garments, and ornaments from those two, casting aside their own personal preferences.
Those whose names describe qualities equal to the beautiful *śrī-rūpa-mañjarī* possess a single line upon their forefeet that surpasses the brilliance of lightning. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.1)
Although he was indeed the personified embodiment of cleverness, nevertheless,
not fully relishing even the status of leader of the herd,
he incessantly bathed in the nectar-ocean of her service.
Standing on the northern side within the inner apartments of her mother-in-law,
she is the radiant abode and the sole repository of the finest artistic skill.
It was constructed by my father Vṛṣabhānu out of affection;
it is the very model itself, and nothing else (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.3).
Where the pillars, porticos, thresholds, courtyards, rows of arches, rafters, various chambers, door-latches,
and altars shine, illuminated by a succession of jewel-lamps.

Where the eaves, possessing the luster of dark clouds, are made of sapphire stones, and the various states of being are like paintings beheld by the eyes of people fashioned with manifold variety. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.4)
That row of swans also shines above, appearing like silver;
seeing which, the peacocks, assuming the attitude of friend toward foe,
spread out their plumage only to contract it again.
There, having wiped, smeared, and purified the various altars used for sitting, reclining, eating, adorning, and so forth— (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.5)— those very [altars].
Having spread out a canopy made of the skins of ranku deer above, those who had gathered together with uplifted joy fastened it in place. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.6)
One woman polished the vessels of gem and gold;
another brought milk suitable for the occasion;
and [another] placed it upon a jeweled couch covered with variegated silken cloths.
On the previous day, he prepared garments, jewels, and ornaments as an additional offering for the object of his meditation. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.7)
There, a certain woman, having loudly unfastened the row of bracelets that were jingling as she opened a casket in which refined substances were placed,
rubbed together camphor, saffron, and sandalwood.
Another, with a joyful mind,
fashioned with flowers alone the various crowns, earrings, armlets, necklaces, and waistbands.
In that interval, some [women] bound fragrant *phaṇivallī* creepers dyed with *jātī*, *lavaṅga*, *khadira*,
and other woods; meanwhile, from every direction, [the scent of] curd-churning arose—
With the sounds of lowing that did not hinder the chanting of the Vedas by the great Brahmins,
and with the herds of calves moving about amidst the obstacles created by the mutual recognition of the groups of cows through their mutual bellowing;
By the waves of nectar from the multitude of titles and the glorious fame of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which are spread forth by the throngs of the most exalted and worshipful devotees— (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.10)
By the warbling of parrots in the groves of *śārī* birds, and by the clamor of sparrows and peacocks, all of which increase in succession;
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.11)
Then, while the multitudes of people were awake— intent on their daily duties during the day— the women lay down, their eyes filled with longing for every moment of Kṛṣṇa.
In the herds whose minds were fixed upon the home of Nanda,
and in her who found her very life in gazing at the lotus-face of her granddaughter—
Having approached there suddenly, [he cried out] to her named Mukharā: "O Rādhā, you who are the casket containing the multitude of jewels of maternal affection! Where are you, my daughter?"
When she calls out, "Are you there?
even though her own nature is crooked, she— [the self]— (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.13).
Then the matted-haired woman, agitated by her desire for the excellence of hearing [the teaching],
approached her and spoke.
O wise one, for the sake of your son’s longevity and the increase of his wealth, you must certainly appoint this daughter-in-law [to the task].
Disregard for the commands of his own cowherd queen regarding auspicious bathing, ornaments, and the like, as well as the worship of the Sun-god for the sake of a million cows.
"Even you show contempt for the words of one ignorant of his duty"—
thus Paurṇamāsī, who understands the true meaning, informed me, she says, day after day.
Therefore, O Noble Lady, bestow upon this your own granddaughter, adorned with every auspicious mark,
so that she may possess all perfections.
"Just as it would be for my son," [he said].

Arise quickly and perform the worship of the site;
having carried out the ritual of the auspicious bath,
offer the articles of worship to the Sun.

With her limbs melting with affection and her voice full of emotion, she entered the bedchamber and said to her:

Have you forgotten today that it is the turn of the Sun?
Having bathed, quickly perform the morning *arghya* rite for him and prepare an offering of worship.
Then, awakened by those words,
Viśākhā rose up, moving languidly.

(Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.50)
Then, by their words, the charming woman was awakened repeatedly upon her bed; she woke again and again,
like one stirred by a multitude of waves in a pond.
Like a royal swan, her limbs languid with passion,
she was at that very moment cognizant of the opportunity.
Ratimañjarī, the companion of the Queen of Vṛndāvana, took hold of her glorious lotus feet.
Thus, having been awakened by many [songs] from her extensive sleep, she arose. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.52)
Then, beholding her with her limbs clad in a beautiful yellow garment,
he spoke these words with a heart full of apprehension:
"This is the evening of Murāri, who possesses the hue of molten gold."
"Viśākhā, why is this garment that your friend wears upon her breast?
Oh, what a mistake! What a blunder!"
Behold this resolve of hers, who is of pure lineage;
her friend, with a startled mind, [held] those words in her heart. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.53–54)
Beholding him in his yellow garment with a sidelong glance,
Viśākhā pointed him out, saying, "Alas, what is this? and immediately spoke to the old woman.
Blinded by their own nature,
they are [overwhelmed] by the abundance of golden-limbed radiance surging forth from the touch of the lattice of sunbeams shining through the openings of the net.

"O charming one, how can you harbor suspicion toward your friend’s dark garment, which has been turned yellow by drinking [the wine], when she is among those of pure intellect? (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.55–56)
Then those friends, headed by Lalitā, came quickly from their respective homes to meet their friend.
With faltering steps,
they approached her; by their words, she was moved.

In the four-pillared pavilions of gold, jewels, and gems upon which they have ascended,

Having understood in her heart that it was the year of the harvest, Śyāmalā, who was well-versed in the conventions of time, approached him at the proper moment;

For indeed, O beautiful one, this [fire], constantly and excessively increasing even when perpetually sprinkled by its friends, [will surely consume you].
O friend, why is it that even now the fruit has not yet been bestowed?

O lotus-faced one, alas, that row of eyelashes was reddened by the juice of her [tears];
yet you did not even see that.

O Śyāma,
you too, though your heart's wound caused by me is entirely unnoticed, laugh at me; therefore, I say this:
"O friend, recognize this: that which lightning destroys in the darkness of night—the blindness of the eyes—it instantly redoubles.

Like a fresh creeper broken by the wind, like a young lotus crushed by an elephant,

Was it a dream, or a magician’s trick, or perhaps a long-lasting delusion?

It became a shattering of the mind and brought about a swoon of the heart.

"Who is this Kṛṣṇa?"— this thought, entering the ear of you, O slender one, dispels my composure.
O you who are blinded by passion! Why do you always play with him as if he were a toy?
Do not mock me, O deluded one;

Truly, truly, he who resembles a flash of lightning has this very day entered the courtyard of her eyes.

Then, her friend stood in profound silence, overcome by the weight of shame, as she held her chin in order to hear the news of her beloved's amorous play.

"Ask about my life, for such is my fortune."
Where indeed could I tell you of those playful gestures when you, O dark-complexioned one, held my very hand? Where were you, who was I, what was that hand, and what did it do? I do not remember.
(Amr̥ta of the Greatness of Vr̥ndāvana 5.98) Oh,
she braids her braid with clusters of divine flowers;

He repeatedly dresses me in divine silk garments and feeds me betel-leaf; yet, though his love for me is such, your friend does not place me upon the bed from his lap. (Vṛndāvana-mahimāmṛtam 5.99)
With unblinking eyes, he constantly holds the moon of his face directly toward my face;

O friend, how can the love of your friend, the jewel of all Nāgaras, be described? (Vṛndāvana-mahimāmṛta 5.97)
O friend, the playful gestures of the destroyer of Keśin,

Virtues cut into the vital organs like wood-worms;

We know not what respect there is for the dignity of the teacher's family in the matter of preserving noble lineage; nor do we have faith in the fiery venom of the words of the wicked; what fear have we?

abandon sleep and become inclined toward wakefulness.

with that soft water from the wish-fulfilling tree, which was most gentle and light, he accepted [the guest-offering].

O King, she— whose palate was sensitive to flavors and who possessed the excellence of the red tint of betel— scratched a beautiful design upon her bracelet of precious gems.

Then, having arrived with the charming sound of her bracelets and anklets,
a certain young maidservant of the prince performed the dressing of his hair, her face brightened by a smile that was free from any ulterior motive.

The cows do not let their milk flow when their calves have departed, nor do they lick them;
with the sound of their lowing filling the circle of the quarters, they are not even now able to endure a moment’s delay.
Thus addressed by someone approaching him,
that cowherd boy [was refreshed] by the nectar-showers of the gentle smiles from the mouths of his own mothers.
Praising his own bliss, he rose up, making his lotus-like face— which was beautifully adorned with betel— exceedingly radiant.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.46)
O Balabhadra, having finished the milk-drinking contest,
if you are going to the arena for the wrestlers along with your younger brother, do not delay.
I worship Your emanation; having spent but a moment with her friends, come quickly to eat together!
(Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 3.47)
Having heard these words of his mother, Hari said: "O Mother, you do not believe me when you speak thus of him alone;
yet, though I am the foremost among them, I am truly but one among these."

(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.48) My child, you are just like a disciplined student.
