the brilliance of Damayantī’s smile surpassed the radiance of a multitude of lightning flashes.
O friend, with a lotus bud held in his resplendent left hand and having been granted a measured amount of gold for milking by his mother, he—
He shone even more than the sun,
with his feet hanging down and mimicking the beauty of the *stambarama* elephant of Vraja. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.50)
With his tiny bells tinkling with the jangling sound of her girdle,
his moon-like face bathed by the waves of the mass of his braid and the luster of his jeweled earrings amidst his swaying locks;
His splendor is exalted by the surging rays from His dense limbs, which shine with the playful dance of His flickering yellow upper garment.
The rising sun of the Kaustubha gem resting upon the circumference of his swaying necklace, with garlands kissing his jingling foot-ornaments.
(Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 3.52)
Having emerged from the delightful city and proceeding forward,
he brought joy to the eyes of his mother and kinsmen, while an unobstructed radiance shone from the chariot borne by his servants.
He reached the top of the city gate,
where he clung to the edge of the outer paved courtyard, his body bristling with horripilation at the thought of Kṛṣṇa. (Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 3.53)
Inquiring "Who is where? What are they doing?
and directing his gaze, he shone resplendent, surrounded by friends who met him with playful jests at the water-jars.
In the lotus-face of Him who understands the nectar of the stories of Karṇa told immediately after his creation, there arose a certain indescribable smile.
Is my mind capable of unraveling even a portion of its meaning? Let your friend, the bee, herself investigate it.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.55)
At that moment, whose mind was not captivated by the great sweetness of his crown’s curvature,
adorned as it was with a network of golden filaments?
O King, how can the weight of the luster of their jewels even be described?
Following after those spreading fragrances are [the sounds of] their anklets and other ornaments.

How many times was he not worshipped by the rows of women moving along the path to Gośāla’s cow-pen, who had ascended the roof-terrace by force with their cries, and who offered him worship with their lotus-like eyes?
Adorned with various playful charms and overflowing with the essence of exquisite beauty,
that beloved Madhurikā is being served to her lover.
She extinguished his fever born of separation, yet she increased that very thirst for her a hundredfold. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.58)
The swelling of joy spread a sense of stillness across her ears,
while the weight of the fever arising from longing entered her eyes;
such was the sudden and incomparable wealth of her neighborly splendor.
She always spreads heat for those who dwell with her;
therefore, she is called Anurāga-parā, the Supreme Devotee of Passionate Love. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.59)
And those very women of beautiful countenance are most blessed, O fair-faced one, who constantly sport with those lovely-eyed ones.
With limbs as bright as polished silver in the ocean of the play of loveliness—
alas, what a birth has been mine in this Gokula! (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 3.60)
Know this: since that sweetness is never embraced by her exceedingly fickle dark heart, not even a fraction of steadfastness can possibly exist here in this worldly existence.
Śyāmā said: "I am going,
Lalitā!"
Listen, I am now going home; let there be an end to my words regarding her.
You, however, go to this Padminī, the consort of the Lord of Vraja’s palace.
"O bee of Kṛṣṇa’s dark eyes, you who are bound by thirst, offer [yourself]!
At that time, she was distressed by separation from her beloved and her intellect had failed. (Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 3.62)
That she perceived even a single moment as an eon of the age,
and that every task was performed for her by her handmaidens,
had its sole cause in the constant practice of what was prescribed for the occasion.
Then, that multitude of all her friends— having been bathed by their own companions and having donned appropriate garments and ornaments—
produced [a splendor] born from the ocean of the rising autumnal moonlight.
One woman brought forth a throne made of the finest jewels, which surpassed even the goddess Śrī with the splendor of Kṛṣṇa’s own lotus feet. (Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 3.64)
Another woman held her sacred footstool beneath her;
one brought the vessels for washing the face, and another set out the implements for cleaning the teeth.
Having risen from the surface of her bed and seated upon a golden throne,
she is now established in a fixed composure as her sleep comes to an end.
Having placed her lotus feet upon the footstool, she shone,
receiving the greetings offered by her excellent attendants.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.49)
By means of the tips of the handles of golden water-pitchers, [the waters] were offered;
having been joined together and gathered into a hollowed cup within the cavity of his mouth,
they possessed a fragrance even more intense than that of his own natural scent.
Reddened by contact with the palms of her glorious lotus hands as she placed them upon the hands of her dear friend,
and thoroughly perfumed with the powder of abundant camphor;
Surrounded by her friends, who were experts in all the arts of dalliance,
she thoroughly cleansed her lotus-face with water.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.50–51)
The water repeatedly scooped up in handfuls from the palm of his hand was moved along until it reached his palate and teeth,
becoming beautiful as it rose through the pair of his moving cheeks.
Scattering her flowing locks over her head, she quietly cast down the vessel filled with sound (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 4.2).
Then, with the hollows of his left hand’s fingers placed above his forehead,
cheeks, and eyes,
he gazed steadily and intently three times at that light which had come from the direction of Sāmita.
Having taken from the celestial tree a garland of golden lotuses, radiant with the luster of its blossoms, which had been placed there by her own companion; (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 4.3)
With her beautiful eyes, she quickly assumed the state of a budding lotus with her very soft hand. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 4.4) (138)
While she was cleansing her teeth, she caused the swinging motion mentioned in the *Pratisara*, the jingling of her bracelets, and the swaying of her earrings.
Then the fair-toothed maiden, having taken up the graceful vine that had sprouted from her ear, assumed the shape of a bow.
From her companion’s hand, out of affection, she received a jeweled girdle that encircles the waist, its two ends held by the pair of fingers of her own soft hands.
Then, with his tongue— which resembles a nine-petaled lotus— he cleanses it while bowing his head with a gentle tremor.
Covering her face with disheveled locks and wearing a gentle smile, she shone forth.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 4.7)
Then,
with her two hands washed and wearing beautiful garments provided by her attendants, she wiped both the exterior and interior of the moon of her face with the edge [of the cloth].
He skillfully removed the drops of water from the jeweled mirror held by his companion. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 4.8)
Seeing him as a witness to her joy,
she bathed his face— which marked the moment of her beloved's arrival— with the nectar of her smile.
Having seen his activities, such as milking the cow and so forth, Kalāvatī arrived.
Then,
filled with supreme joy,
Gopāla also spoke near him regarding his own cow-pen.
Accompanied by Sarāma and Madhumaṅgala, and with Kāvya-Gīṣpati as his companion, he entered the sky like the evening moon.
Surrounded by a white canopy, Rāma bore the celestial beings [upon his shoulders].
Causing the illusion of being Airāvata standing amidst the rows of the great boulders of Kailāsa.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.38)
In the midst of the rows of white lotuses standing all around, Acyuta, rising up, appeared to the people like a blossoming white lotus.
He [experienced] the illusion of bees moving from one row of lotuses to another;
"Hihī! Gaṅgā! Godāvarī! (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.39).
O speckled one!
O Kālindī! O white one!
Hīhī, O smoky one!
Tūṅgi, Bhramari, Yamunā.
Haṃsi! Kamale! Hihī Rambhe! Campe!
"O female elephant! O doe!
thus did that protector of the cowherds repeatedly call out the names of all the cows.
With her limbs resting upon her forefeet and her knees striking against each other,
she herself milks one cow; meanwhile, others, with faces upturned, cause her to milk the rest by their own efforts.
Satisfying her own herd of calves by scratching them, she causes the others to drink;
thus the son of Nanda rejoices at dawn, delighting his mother-in-law.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.41)

With sandals placed upon the tips of his feet and his heels shining with the upward radiance of his three-fold arch, he rests his buttocks between his knees; as he bows low, saying "Pa Onnam," his crown-protuberance becomes loosened by the gentle agitation of the beautiful opening formed by the crossing of his thighs, which emit a rising luster.
With his two hands, Hari milks the earth, whose blossoming fingers are like sprouts;
[he who is] dearer to the Blessed One even than a calf, through the touch of his lotus-like hands. (Ānanda-vṛndāvana-campū 11.88)
The cow, whose udders were streaming with milk, being milked herself,
filled the milking vessel with streams of milk that resounded with a deep and profound roar; she then leaped up as high as the earth itself, reaching from the vessel to the space beyond it.
With his fingers restrained by the tip of his thumb, his foot partially covering the ground,
and rubbing the hem of his garment, he stands here before us with two or three drops of milk.
O friend, Dāmodara milks the cow, the sound of the trickling stream within the mouth of the pot, which is held between his two knees, being most enchanting.
Hearing [the music], she forgot the act of bathing due to her helplessness of emotion.
With an agitated mind, Lavaṅgamañjarī immediately offered oblations there upon a soft, golden seat.
As she sat reclining, covered by a garment of fine Chinese silk,
her skilled attendants quickly surrounded her, bearing offerings.
Lalitā gently took the collection of ornaments from her friend’s body and placed it upon her own.
Like a cluster of tender leaves, flowers, and blossoms from a golden vine, [he was] full of affection. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.60)
Having wiped his entire body— which was marked with the scars of the battle against the bodiless Love— with a fragment of cloth from his excellent garment,
she dressed him at night in a robe smeared with unguents.
Having drawn away the charming veil from her head, he removed her garment, which was endowed with unsurpassed fragrance.
Having loosened their masses of hair, those women with beautiful heads,
with rows of moving bracelets, affectionately and respectfully purified themselves with jeweled ornaments.
Having washed her two feet and displayed a mirror before her, a certain woman, praised for her skill in the arts, [prepared herself].
With abundant affection, he anointed the lotus-faced one with his glistening youth, which was like a fragrant and excellent unguent. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.56)

Whenever she lifted her beautiful garment from one limb or another, she would feel bashful upon seeing it; thus, she repeatedly applied ointment to that limb, saying to her friend, "Look, it has been smeared! and then, "It has been smeared! again.
Her companions, their hearts intensely pure with affection, anointed her entire body— which had already been stripped of its modesty— with oil.
They performed a body massage for her from the soles of her feet to the crown of her head,
using an ointment made of fragrant powders of camphor, musk, saffron, and sandalwood.
Having cleansed the hair by rubbing it with various means using the fragrant, pure, and stainless decoction of *āmalakī* fruits, [she prepared it]. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.58)
He sprinkled [the ground] with graceful water-pots dripping from their necks,
as if out of a natural bond of affection.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.59)
By two [vases], filled with water scented with camphor appropriate for the occasion and drawn from jars made of various lordly gems, which were being slowly poured from both sides.
They both sprinkled Sumukhī with water on her two sides,
and having firmly wrapped her beautiful locks with a garment, (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.60).
Having wrung it out until much water flowed, having squeezed it thoroughly,
and having spread it out again with her moving fingers, she scattered it once more and then bound the garment after unfolding it.
One fortunate woman wiped her moon-like face, another her throat-base, and yet another her ears with a soft cloth. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.61)
What is the chest, what is the back, and what are the two arms? What is most excellent and supremely beautiful?
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.62)

Having wrapped [her] in a dry garment, he lifted her from the ground so that she would not sit down; then, wiping the flowing water from her lower garment with both hands, he slowly and gracefully led her away.
He fastened the *ardhoruka* garment around his hips, which remained motionless upon his excellent, rubbed-down breasts. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.63)
Then a certain woman, skilled in the arts,
fastened a bodice made of fine cloth by her own companions,
who were experts in various extraordinary crafts.
Above that, rising from a shimmering *caṇḍātaka* of waves, there is a very thin, deep red garment with upward-flying rays of light.
He fastened his garment, which was bound with golden threads and kissed by the tips of the moon-like nails of the lotus-feet of Śrī.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.65)
With a pair of long, hanging, well-woven silk cords,
radiant with the luster of the finest pearls and possessing a shimmering majesty,
[the elephant’s trunk] assumes a resemblance to a lotus through the process of its contraction.
She tied her girdle, which was the very essence of exquisite craftsmanship,
just above her navel;
it was like a fresh śārikā bird adorned with golden spots.
The intense luster above that shone most brilliantly;
its very envelopment is called the unimpeded obstruction of Mukunda’s vision.
Then,
having ascended it, she was seated upon the surface of a great jeweled throne, which was covered with a spread of extremely soft cloth.
Having joyfully washed her two lotus-feet, the friends adorned her with various auspicious garments and ornaments. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.67)
Having extended it further many times, having adorned it repeatedly with many jewel ornaments, and having purified it by means of the fingers,
he set forth the pervasive flow of incense produced from black agallochum.
The female companions made her mass of hair fragrant by straightening it from its state after bathing and arranging it with beautiful curls.
Having drawn a tilaka with musk upon her forehead, she fashioned a young braid adorned with a dot of vermilion at the parting of her hair, which was as delightful as the rays of a great jewel.

Adorned on both sides up to the temples with an array of musk-leaf patterns, and surrounded on the forehead by a cluster of sandalwood dots, it is known as the "Machine of Desire. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.69)

Then, she fashioned a tilaka marked with a parting line, its interior adorned with musk, rising sandalwood paste, and a crescent of moon, and further embellished with thick streaks of vermilion paste. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.77)
Upon his head he bound a crest-jewel of the finest gems,
which possessed the luster of the heart of a fine mālatī flower,
and his braided hair was encircled by a shimmering band of red silk.
With a pair of long, hanging [pendants] possessing the luster of the lord of jewels,
[resembling] a golden rod inserted into a minute upper aperture.
In the region between the ears, where the root and tip meet in graceful union, the two Śrī-cakrikā and Bakulikā of beautiful form bestow instruction,
bearing the weight of a mass of jewel-like radiance.
With a strand of pearls, she fashioned a leaf-patterned ornament at the edge of her curls, which was beautifully illuminated by its shimmering light.
A certain woman fashioned a most magnificent pair of earrings made of the finest gems for each of his two ears.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.72)
One woman, having adorned her eyes with crushed collyrium as if they were the two arrows of the God of Love ground with mercury, placed a pearl upon the left side of her nose.
With her soft cheeks darkened by the weight of the luster of collyrium and her lower lip, she draws a sea-monster [design] upon them. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.73)
Even as she was summoning the one whose banner is the makara, Hari, offering her lip— a sprout red as dawn— should worship him at that moment of aesthetic essence.
In the center of her beautiful chin, there shines the mark made by the two fingers of His hand, fashioned like a needle of the king of jewels. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛtam 4.68) (178)
A drop of fresh musk, beautifying her glorious moon-like face,
is like a bee settled upon the tip of a lotus petal.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.83)
Having anointed the face of this Viśākhā with sandalwood paste mixed with camphor, agallochum, and saffron;
The back, the arms, the breasts,
and the chest [are adorned] with flower clusters, crescent moons, and lotuses. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.76)
She drew a wonderful makara and mango sprout upon the slopes of her breasts with musk in a variegated design.
Under the guise of fish, flowers, fresh sprouts, and the crescent moon, Kāma [carries] his own emblems: arrows, spears, and bows. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.78)
I believe that he, whose karma was dispelled by the mere movement of her bow-like eyebrows, deposited [his senses] within the dwelling of her own breast-cups.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.79)
Her breasts are covered with various jewels and pearls set in a mosaic, adorned with a red silk bodice,
and variegated like a rainbow.
Like two mountains covered by the glow of twilight,
they shone above, adorned with lattices of various inlaid jewels.
In the city of Vimalā, Viśākhā suddenly covered with her apron the neck of that lotus-eyed woman— which bore the beauty of the marks left by Hari’s hand—
fearing, as it were, the Lord himself. It hid it within her own bosom.
Adorned with diamonds and variegated with jewels,
its thick middle bound by cords of fine thread,
it shone near the hollow of her throat.
Alas! She has given away that wonderful swan,
shining between a pair of golden balls (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.86–87).
A necklace named *gostana*— swallowed by a *masāra* gem and interspersed at intervals with very fine strings of pearls— was fastened upon her heart by her.
With the spaces between them strung with beads of emerald, moonstone, ruby, and gold spheres.
She fastened that jewel garland, interwoven with pearls and corals, upon his heart.
(Govindalīlāmṛta 2.89)
A golden bowl set with pairs of lapis lazuli,
containing seed-like globules, with clusters of variegated pearl necklaces swallowed at intervals within it.
In the heart of her who was dancing and singing together with him during the midnight *rāsa*, he, being placed by her, shone brilliantly. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.90)
With a pleased heart, she placed upon his chest the garland of *guñjā* berries, which had been given by Hari from his own neck as if it were royal fortune itself manifest before his very eyes.
Beautiful with rows of thick stars and adorned by an excellent leader.
Her single-string necklace adorned the sky of her heart like moonlight.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.92)
A slender golden city, its interior filled with emeralds set amidst rubies encrusted with gold-inlaid diamonds, with chains hanging down from its royal turrets.
At the time of the playful adornment by her circle of friends, a four-sided couch joined with Viśākhā was present in her heart. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.93)
As she was being adorned with a magnificent necklace of great sapphire gems, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu became perspired,
trembling, and covered in horripilation.

At that time, the net of yak-tail hair, pure and hanging in succession from the end of her back— serving as a binding cord for the strings of pearl necklaces at the end of her neck— shone brilliantly upon her face.
I believe that, out of compassion, the Creator clearly fashioned a staircase for the serpent-like braid to ascend to the mountain of her beautiful hips (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.94).
On his upper arm was an incomparable armlet set with precious gems; on his forearm were incomparable bracelets;
and at their junction was a certain auspicious thread-band fastened there.
Exceedingly wonderful with its jeweled setting that radiates the luster of gems (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.75), [it is adorned] with a pearl necklace and armlets studded with *muktāvalī* pearls.
Enveloped by the arrangement of rows of bracelets,
and joined by the orbs of the moon and the sun, his arm shines intensely like Rahu himself.
Marked with his own name and intermingled with the luster of various jewels. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.97)
Her finger-ring appeared as the crusher of the pride of her adversaries.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.99)
At the base of her abdomen, she wears a girdle-string fashioned from jewels with a jeweled clasp at the front; below that, there is a cluster of jewels;
and upon her toes, she wears rings made of excellent gems.
The friend (Kṛṣṇā) has donned a pair of beautiful anklets reaching down to her ankles;
from her toenails to the tips of her hair and across the soles of her feet, there is a great crimson glow.
Ahaha! Has your state not turned to the color of barley-gruel? Have men not performed the great festival of the sun with the light of a trembling lamp?
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛtam 4.96) Another said:
"You have applied red lac to Your lotus feet in vain."
His own passion alone is the elixir for the eyes;
yet he possesses one unique quality, O Rādhikā,
which even colors the hair of Keśava.
And a certain woman fastened a pair of anklets, fashioned from exceedingly beautiful jewels, upon her lotus-like feet.
To demonstrate her own skill in various arts, one girl brought a mirror made of the finest gems before him.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.78)
Then, at dawn, the garland-maker placed upon the lotus-hand of Viśākhā— whose face was a smiling lotus— the offering brought by his own friend, the slender Jayā, through Narmadā.
The play-lotus of the lotus-eyed one; she [assumed] a form and attire suited to the curiosity of Kṛṣṇa’s eyes. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 2.103)
Beholding their own tall forms reflected in the mirror, those beautiful women became restless with the desire to approach Kṛṣṇa;
for indeed, exquisite attire has as its fruit the sight of one's beloved.
In the midst of that [pastime], he engaged in the sport of wrestling and other such activities together with his friends.
Upon seeing her, whose body was golden-hued,
as she approached, he quickly ceased from milking the cow and spoke with charming gestures.
Together with her own dear friends of similar character,
she went with one accord to the jeweled hall of constant practice for the playful exercises of the curious wrestler.
Then,
with these friends of his own age, he engaged in wrestling matches, limb-to-limb, each one individually and without fear.
By manifesting their respective prowess, with anger and pride, they acted through serpents that slithered, crawled, and glided away.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.21)
Then, having rested for a while, with certain roots of the great tree of virtue— those very accumulations of merit gathered by them—
they [prepared] for the purpose of anointing with charming smiles of endearment.
He entered the auspicious bathhouse for anointing with servants who were skilled in the application of various compositions and many binding techniques. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.22)

Though it was undertaken by him, that [anointing] which had been properly commenced with oil by the simple-minded— [an oil] being a most auspicious fragrant kinsman— in the specialized arts of auspicious massage, was not accepted by him.
From head to foot, with all their fortunes intact,
they were anointed with oils fit for honoring a beloved assembly.
Then, with affection, they long and repeatedly pressed those limbs of his, neither too loosely nor too firmly, which were most auspicious. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.24)
Then, removing the state of witheredness caused by oil with saffron powder and fine camphor dust, which was soft and pleasant when ground together until finely crushed;
They massaged those limbs of Kṛṣṇa with some fragrant substance,
exquisitely scented with camphor.
With jars filled with various kinds of crystal and gold,
the group of young maidservants bathed the lotus-eyed girl, arranging her hair which had been cleansed by astringent decoctions.
One woman repeatedly scratched her hair, which was stained with astringent dye;
another gently stroked her tender limbs.
Sprinkling water with a golden pitcher, she attained an exceedingly great splendor of passion. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.27)
Is it a fresh rain-cloud with moonbeams, or a blue thread with white;
is it a sprout of sapphire with the waters of the luster of pure crystal gems,
or a young *tamāla* tree bathed in pearls that shines forth so brilliantly?

Or rather, is it a dark blue lotus? Murāri’s body is like this, having been completed with bright powders of the moon; who indeed would perform its bathing with auspicious water from a conch-shell placed upon the head?
Then, having brought forth many cloths for rubbing the limbs,
they performed his thorough cleansing by massaging him with great care.
First they wiped [the body] with soft, unbleached pieces of fine cloth,
and afterwards, in due order, with white, fine, and dry cloths, [cleansing it] from the feet up to the mass of hair at every joint.
They performed their cleansing, attended by acts of affection; some, with their hair still wet, [dried it] with two kinds of garments— (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.29).
Khaṇḍa, with a gentle and slow smile,
skillfully drew the garment falling from his waist up to his throat;
though he acted with indifference, he guided it back within the folds of his cloth.
A pair of silken garments, yellow like molten gold, was brought with great haste by someone as a new gift.
Having quickly cast aside the previous cloth offered by someone onto his lotus-like hand, he immediately put on another (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.31).
While he was thus seated, his lotus-feet washed and his radiant body shining,
a certain attendant of the prince who had followed behind him—
The mass of hair was not skillfully managed in its task;
rather, having repeatedly spread it out, wiped it, and adorned it, [it remained so].
Having been cleansed many times with a jeweled comb and then covered with a piece of cloth, that mass of hair, bound with two locks, shone forth with splendor.
The dark-blue hue of her hair, produced by their mutual protection, and the whiteness of her exceedingly fine garment; (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.33)
This arrangement of his hair is like one who has just cast off his slough after enjoying another; for into whose eyes has it not entered?
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.34)
Then, having straightened her naturally curly locks and curled them into beautiful braids, she painted upon her forehead a tilaka with the luster of the moon's orb.
Possessing a beautiful luster from the essence of sandalwood and saffron (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.35),
[it is adorned] with emeralds, sapphires, diamonds, and rubies—
He wore the great lord of jewels named Śrī-kaustubha, which, though itself sinless, eclipses even the moon by its brilliance and is dense with rays that cause the luster of others to fade.
She wore necklaces fashioned from a thick cluster of pearl fruits that had reached a state beyond the range of speech.
One [garland] upon his broad chest, another at the region of his navel, and yet another hanging down at the base of his knees.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.37)
He placed upon her ears two jeweled earrings shaped like crocodiles, which,
by the radiance of their luster, spread a great splendor across her cheeks that were moist with water.

Having set aside the previous [ornaments] by means of the bathing festival, he [donned] two most beautiful long pendants made of excellent silk thread (*satpaṭṭasūtra*)— (from the *Kṛṣṇāhnikakaumudī* 2.38).
Someone fastened two armlets at the joints of his wrists— armlets made of the nine gems, such as emeralds and others, which kissed auspicious threads fashioned from cloths of the six precious jewels.
A magnificent divine ring, transformed by the splendor of that ruby, was placed upon her ring finger.
Someone gave him a captivating jeweled seal on his back, which was impossible to refuse, while holding it threateningly between the forefinger and thumb. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.40)

At the base of her thighs, there is a string of ruby bells, attached by a connection fashioned from various excellent jewels, extending along the belly toward the waistband of her yellow silk garment.
Someone bound upon her lotus-feet, which were adorned with shimmering silk garments, a crest-jewel fashioned from the finest of gems.
Then, having placed a pair of anklets shimmering with the moonlight of her toenails,
someone held up a magnificent jeweled mirror over her moon-like face with longing.
In the meantime, a certain person, taking the command of the Lord of Vraja, entered his house.
And Kṛṣṇa said: "O Janaka, by your word, you ought to give ten thousand cows to many twice-born brahmins."
Having heard his father’s words, he bound up his hair, properly adjusted his yellow upper garment, and then thoroughly purified himself.
Having sipped water for purification, Rāmānuja— whose face was radiant and who was a mountain of the jewels of virtue— bestowed cows with a mind fixed on Śiva.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 2.44)
The most desired [food] for Goṣṭheśvarī, a delicious cooked meal,
was prepared; however, she was unable to endure the delay while it was being cooked through many stages.
Then, without delay, she sent some food to be eaten,
consisting of fresh butter, curd, milk, lakes of [sweetened] milk, and other delicacies.
Having consumed this mixture of camphor powder and having sipped water for purification, he whose moon-like face was sweet took betel, leaning upon the shoulder of his dear friend.

The playful nectar-sports of the *Pīyūṣagranthi* and the camphor-like *Karpūra*.

(From *Govinda-līlāmṛta* 3.99) There were balls of aged *kuṣmāṇḍa* gourds along with *kacvī*, *mānalu*, and tubers.
Others were prepared, enriched with a powder seasoned with bitter [ingredients] and abundant with cavikā.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 3.100)
By combining this with sugar, cardamom,

The sweet dish called *kṣīra-kuṣmāṇḍa* (3.101) and the sweet *dadhi-śūraṇaka*.
One part of dhātrī and śūraṇaka,

This black-stalked potherb (nālīta), when cooked with its juices, provides relish;

Now,

However, some things must be done;
therefore, consider our food and condiments already prepared.
Seeing all that— fragrant, of excellent color, and enchanting— she became filled with joy.
Then Rohiṇī, with wonder, spoke to her who was desiring to know the ritual procedure for that:
"The collection of materials is indeed the same."
This is indeed the process of ripening;
however, it is the cause of a new quality,

She [Kālindī] saw Rādhā, intent on preparing the food,
perspiring and with her face bowed down in modesty.
Seeing her, the queen, her heart melting with affection,
commanded her maidservant to fan her.
(Govindalīlāmṛta 3.112)
Now, he describes her skill in serving:
when the dining area was covered with cloth, rows of jewel-caskets containing various kinds of precious side-dishes were arranged in order all around before the glorious jewel-throne.

Outside of those was a row of small boxes filled with a multitude of sweet, desired, well-ground flour-cakes; and outside of those was a row of small golden boxes made of excellent, auspicious cow-hide— thus,
in this wondrous manner, arranged in successive rows in the shape of a half-moon.
By her handmaidens, through various arrangements of many beautiful and variegated patterns,
a lovely golden vessel was placed in the center, filled with auspicious boiled rice and served with fine, fragrant, smooth, and glistening drops of clarified butter that did not cling to one another.
A golden shallow dish [filled] with ghee, *puṭapāka*, sugar-candy, and so forth,
together with ripe mango pieces and other ingredients such as *satkāsamarda* that are moistened with a binding liquid.
Having placed the appropriate [offering] to her right, he set down golden water-pitchers near her, filled with water highly perfumed with camphor. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 3.3)

Having observed her manifold skill in cooking and the wonderful arrangement of their food service, the beloved of the Lord of Vraja, her heart overflowing with wonder and affectionate in mind, sent for both Kṛṣṇa and Rāma.
Then, out of the power of their intense faith, those two approached the foster-mother directly; having bowed to his mother, he, together with Balarāma, brought her great joy by her command.
Having washed the two lotus-feet made by the young maidservant with love,

and having sipped water for purification, he sat down facing her; and as he gazed at all those various offerings before him from a beautiful food-vessel, the one clad in yellow garments shone forth with a mind filled with wonder.
To his left are Śrīdāman and Subala,
and in front of him is Madhumangala.
To the right sat Śrībala, and others sat around him on all sides.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.22)
For he began to eat by the path shown in succession by his two mothers;
whatever he attempted to eat, he could not bear to leave it,
desiring to consume each and every thing in its entirety, being himself capable of doing so.
Out of fear of being observed while eating even a little, and out of fear of malicious gossip,
this [skill] of cooking was displayed by those who eat together, those who explain [the texts] together, and those with their forces, along with the cooks. (Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 3.7)

Eating with relish, he spoke even with his heart; praising it, he first ate his fill of milk-rice. Then, seeing that there was not enough for others, he became filled with intense greed, striving for more of that jewel among side-dishes.

Just as a cook may please his mother by eating all kinds of fine side dishes, satisfying her through the sequence of vegetables and so forth, so too [does one act] for the sake of pleasing the Mother.
Smiling and making them laugh with charming speech, he said to all those who were eating together, "Eat; do not leave anything behind," thus bringing them singular joy.
(Kṛṣṇāhnika-kaumudī 3.9)
Summoned by her, they brought their own various prepared delicacies suitable for the morning meal.
The cowherd girls, filled with joy,
[brought] from the house with great effort by Śrī Rādhā for her mother... (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.24)
Then, at her mother's gesture, Raṅgadevī brought forth sweetmeat balls made from imported sugar, which were called "water of the Gaṅgā."
The mother divided those among Balarāma and the others and gave them to them out of affection. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.25)
Having placed [the offerings] separately in scattered golden vessels (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.26).
Relishing food cooked in ghee,
making even them laugh with his excellent jests,
and looking at them with the corners of his eyes.
The noble women joyfully beheld that face of Rādhā, [exclaiming], "This is auspicious!
This is sweet! (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.27).
Pointing with her forefinger at that which was glossy and very beautiful, the mother said, "Eat this, my child."
(From the *Govinda-līlāmṛta* 4.28:
Whatever may be dear to anyone,
knowing that again and again, Hari laughs.
To each of them he gave that very thing, repeatedly casting it from his own vessel.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.29)
Seeing his mother intent on her efforts and Acyuta eating slowly, he,
who was skilled in jesting, [acted] toward him...
The boy said to the mistress of Vraja:
"O Mother, if he does not eat much, give me everything; I shall eat it."
Embraced and nourished by me alone,
who am a consumer of abundant food, this one of dull luster will have no power [to digest].
O Mother, since he is accustomed to eating food cooked with ghee, have light, well-prepared food and side dishes given to him.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.30–32) Then Kṛṣṇa, laughing, [offered] handfuls of cooked food from his own vessel.
With five or six [mouthfuls], he filled the boy's bowl, saying, "Eat. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.33)
Then, sounding his own left elbow, he properly began to eat on his left side.
Delighted, the young brahmin said to him,
"Friend, look! While saying 'I shall eat,' he is eating two mouthfuls."
"Mother, give me yogurt," he said,
and sent her to fetch it.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.34–35)
"O cowherds, look! Here dances this restless monkey-king, greedy for curd and intent on obtaining cooked food"— having made them look up in that direction with these words,
he slowly dropped his own food into their eating vessels.
"I have eaten all of this," he said again with pride to her,
who had approached him with a vessel of curd in her hand. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.36)
He said, "Look, Mother!
I have consumed it all very quickly, even without the curd."
Have that abundant milk-rice given to me,
placed in golden vessels by Rādhā. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.37)
Rohiṇī quickly gave them the milk-rice, which had been cooled by the gentle breezes from fresh plantain leaves and placed in her own hand.
Bringing back one after another the various side-dishes provided by the Gandharvas, she...
He gave them vegetables and other items that had become sour,
distributing them to them gradually and sparingly.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.40)
With the color and lightness of the inner petals of a lotus,
and resembling finely ground flour of polished wheat,
they were served by her after being sprinkled with ghee.
Having first set aside cooked food for them, she placed it in other vessels and gave it to them (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.41).
Furthermore, the humorous remark made to the boy regarding food and such would not constitute a redundancy here.
Kṛṣṇa was full of thirst, while Bala ate nothing more than mouthfuls;
Śrīdāmā, by name, was one who ate sparingly.
"Subala is abandoned by Asubala" (Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 6.45); where is this [state] of their single-minded focus on eating?
Where is this lack of discernment and ignorance? This food, which mocks nectar,
has been prepared by Lakṣmī herself.
Does poetry composed by a true poet not become fruitless? (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛtam 6.46)
In that assembly where there is no greed for its taste (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.47).
This fourfold food is the personified fruit of the four aims of life;
I alone am its sole master.
"A bowl," said the young brahmin boy;
Śrī Dāma replied, "With balls of rice. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.48)
Quickly fill your belly with that which is your entire wealth,
for the sake of which you have assumed the state of a religious student.
The young brahmin said, "O fool!
You are but a cowherd; what indeed do you know?"
Wander through the forest to graze the cows for the sake of your own dharma, tasting the nectar of rasa.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.50)
Behold! I am this learned brahmin; by those who have offered oblations into my mouth, all sacrifices have been performed.
The Blessed Lord alone is the sole authority for both Śruti and Smṛti regarding the liberation from bondage (Śrīdāma-ukti). (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.51)
Even though you have been familiar with the path for a hundred births, it is only the Sūtra that has truly become yours in this state of being a Brahmin.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛtam 6.52) Kṛṣṇa said to the boy, "You have practiced the science of aesthetic relish."
Because one possesses expertise in the various word-forms, intended meanings, and figurative indications [of the scriptures] (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.53).
The young student said: "In my opinion, there are only six rasas here, not eight;
it is logical that the aesthetic experience (āsvāda) is indeed sixfold."
They say that we have only six senses, for there are eight objects of taste. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.54)
Even those who rely upon the phonemes possess not even a trace of proficiency in the phonemes; indeed, such proficiency does not exist for them.
Having abandoned vegetables, soups, and the like,
they suckle that which is in the sky.
Abandoning that manifest water, they run toward the mirage alone.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.57)
They have declared that the cause for the production of rasa is through *carvaṇa* (chewing); for they will experience [rasa] by means of this chewing.
Rāma said regarding the tasting of rasa: "Not even through ten million births from a father" (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.58).
In your system, what are the transitory emotions (anubhāvas),
what are the evanescent moods (sañcāriṇas), and what is the stable emotion (sthāyī)? How is that [stable emotion] tasted?
The young brahmin said: "Because of not attaining that [Lord],
tears would already have come to my eyes even before now."
But through the attainment of this very manifestation, there arise horripilation and a serene countenance.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.60)
The luster of one's complexion arises from smoothness and satisfaction, while its loss leads to pallor; behold this for yourself as I speak even while eating.
Because of that, my voice is broken;
I have great paralysis from eating sweet foods.
Perspiration arises from the suffering of being unable to eat, but at the end,
dissolution results from eating too much.
In this state, laziness, anxiety, sleep, and so forth are clearly our transitory mental states (sañcāri-bhāvas). (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛtam 6.62)
Although there is only one permanent emotion by virtue of being the object of relish, it nevertheless bears various names. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.63)
I think these rice-grains, anointed with ghee, possess a fragrance as if they have been bathed in golden water.
To whomsoever accessibility was granted within the assembly of cowherds, who smelled the fodder and other things cut with a cow's tusk.
For me, who has performed meritorious deeds and partakes in abundant enjoyments, [this has come] by way of association. (Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta 6.70–71)
In the forest, the Brahmins perform austerities, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits;
you, O boy, have no right there.
"O friend, perform austerity while enjoying worldly pleasures; for it is true that by those who have performed austerity in the past," (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.72) "enjoyment was attained."
Having been transformed here in this birth into condiments for me by means of leaves, roots, fruits, and so forth;
"Know this: that which was enjoyed daily by those who dwell on earth and in heaven is now clearly manifest."
Without performing austerities, how can one attain this?
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.73–74) If it is thus, then first [one must perform austerities].
These monkeys are worthy;
even in this birth, they are ascetics who exert themselves through the labor of their speech.
Enduring cold, heat, and wind,
they subsist on leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Why should they not remember their past births? Who can truly know their realized wisdom? (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.80)
Kṛṇa said, "Friend,
these brāhmaṇas are solely intent on the worship of Brahman, while these monkeys are merely filling their bellies."
I perceive a vast difference between these two: [the devotee] and this monkey.
O Hari, there is no difference whatsoever between them; whether it be the state of a human or the state of a monkey,
there is no cause for distinction between these two.
Moreover,
by proclaiming that [deed], he manifested his own unprecedented expertise in the world.
Because of its vastness and because it nourishes,
one's own belly is considered to be Brahman.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.83)
Therefore, for him who meditates three times a day, that very [Brahman] is worshipped by him as the means of fulfillment.
By a lifelong celibate student (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī),
[it is said in Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.84:
"Sometimes [he may eat] abundant cooked food..."
Through the agitation of devouring and entering [the victim], he acts like a monkey;
and through the lightness of his hands while eating, he becomes like a monkey.
Having spoken thus,
that young boy Subala laughed at them all.
While laughing as he ate,
his face turned crimson from the loud sounds of the *kāśa* grass.
(Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.86)
"O cowherd boy, lord of the herd!
Stay for a moment; do not eat, do not laugh; attain steadiness and do not chatter."
"O children, do not make him laugh," [said Nanda],
regarding that which was refined by Lalitā and others through Dhaniṣṭhā. (Kṛṣṇa-bhāvanāmṛta 6.87)
Placing various delicacies such as *rasālā* before them in separate vessels, the Queen of Vraja joyfully gave them to these [cowherds] with affection.
Delighted by the sight of the face of their heart’s beloved,
they were drawn away by its exceedingly sweet, soft, and lovely luster.
Overwhelmed by the vastness of their newly awakened love,
those women, highly praised, went to the house of their lover.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.43)
Furthermore, they tasted those four kinds of foods with longing, as if they were the sweet transformations arising from the essence of nectar.
Making him laugh with jests, they laughed; some chewed soft, tasty morsels. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.44)
Others greedily lick various foods to be licked; others, filled with joy, drink beverages; and still others, insatiable, suck and chew various foods to be sucked and chewed.
The lotus-eyed Lord, with longing, ate that various food very slowly from the touch of his beloved's hand, exclaiming "How delicious! as it was sweeter than nectar.
With the bees of the corners of his eyes fixed upon her lotus-face,
he tasted it deeply and spread a dense joy within his mother’s heart.
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.46)

Nourished by the tasting of the nectar of her extreme loveliness, which was met through the channel of glances from the corners of her eyes cast with timid curiosity, she veiled the expanding exultation of all-embracing emotion.
Rādhikā also loudly addressed the heart of her beloved; then,
placing that mother of Balarāma in between them, he began to dance.

Seeing his beloved offering him sweet food very gently while holding in her hand a woman with eyes languid with intoxication, Kṛṣṇa, the lord of connoisseurs, became slack in his desire for eating and grew restless.
How much was eaten by him,
and how much remained as three parts?
Seeing that he was slow in eating upon beholding the food, his mother became anxious. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.49)
"My son, why have you abandoned all the food and other provisions that were prepared with such great effort? You are hungry; eat as much as you can."
"By my oath upon my own head," [he said],
having brought the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu with great effort. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.50)
All this—food and the like, sweet as the highest nectar—has been prepared by your daughter; yet you do not eat it. What can I do, wretched woman that I am?
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.51) Then she said to Rohiṇī:
"Look, Rohiṇī! He is fickle."
Though weak and hungry, he eats nothing at all, for he is a slow eater.
(Govindalīlāmṛta 4.52)
Then this mother, her limbs overwhelmed with affection,
fondled the Destroyer of Sins (Kṛṣṇa),
the slayer of Pralamba.
Standing before him, she spoke to him with effort: "O child, this delicious food has been prepared by me with Mallī flowers as soft as butter."
You are emaciated by hunger, yet you do not eat;
why then do you cause distress to this mother, to me, and to yourself?
(Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.53–54)
"Look, my son, your mother is distressed; I am going there to cleanse you,
for as you wander in the forest, you will surely become weary."
"Eat as much as you wish; follow my word.
"I have eaten much; my hunger has passed. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.55)
Having spoken thus and restrained his surging agitation,
the two mothers rejoiced upon seeing the son of Nanda looking at them again with a gentle smile.
"Child,
eat this, this most delicious thing," says the mother.
Then, pointing with her fingers to each thing while swearing oaths,
she, her eyes overflowing with tears, desires to do everything; she speaks of that food gone into her womb as being together with her son.
Rasālā, ripe mango juice, śikhariṇī, ṣāḍava, milk,
karambha, āmikṣā, side dishes, curd, fruit cakes, and vegetables.
Though her garment was drenched by the milk flowing from her breasts as she repeatedly suckled him, she remained unsatiated; then, she fed her son who was already full. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.58)
Having eaten and drunk an abundance of food— hard and soft, sweet, lickable, and drinkable— that was soft and sweet, they were satiated by the fullness of its flavor.
All became eager to go to the forest;
all [anointed] their lotus-like faces and hands with fragrant clay.
Having thoroughly cleansed their teeth with a soft brush,
they then performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana) with water provided by the servants from golden and other vessels.
With small pellets of excellent khadira wood provided by Jambūla, mixed with cardamom, cloves, and camphor; (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.60)
Having joyfully fanned your face with cool, radiant breezes, they wiped your belly full [of food] with their left hand. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.61)
Then, while still eagerly chewing with great comfort the rolls of well-ripened betel leaves offered by the hands of their lovers,
they rested upon spacious couches interspersed with bees.
Then they rested in the houses, fanned by their attendants;
there, the servants [waited upon] him who had taken rest.
Fanning the Lord with fans made of peacock feathers, the playful attendant then offered him soft betel rolls after having crushed the leaf.
Having emerged from the kitchen with her feet and hands washed,
she was attended by groups of maidservants with fans.

The Queen of Vraja gazed from the window at her lover, who was standing within the inner courtyard with his friends, while Rādhā looked on from the window; she was drenched by the sweat born of bliss.
Perceiving that she was exhausted by fatigue,
Balāmbā joyfully had her sit down and, with great effort, had food brought from the house so that she might eat.
Directed by her [the goddess], Dhaniṣṭhā was to give food prepared with ghee along with the remnants of what Hari had eaten.
Having mixed it secretly with foods prepared with ghee,
he brought it from his house and gave it to them.

Seeing Rādhikā not eating, her face bowed down and covered by her garment out of modesty, Kṛṣṇa spoke to her.
My mother, overwhelmed with maternal affection; O Mother, why would such a one feel shame before me? My heart feels excessive tenderness for you, as if you were my own son.
"O, remove her! I am going; perform a ritual cleansing for you. Cool my eyes; enjoy [her], for I see her directly. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.67–68)
"And you are my sons; why, out of this shame, do you daughters—Lalitā and the others—not eat?
Thus, through her insistence and hundreds of oaths, the mother [persuaded them].
She fed them with sweet foods and sweet words;
then, with their respective pairs of lotus-hands washed by maidservants... (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.69)

Having washed their faces with water mixed with camphor and wiped them dry with their own garments, those women— fair as excellent gold, separated from the moon [of their husbands] by the night— enjoyed the moonlight provided by their attendants.
Those [ornaments], which were acquired with great effort together with many such [others], through the intense longing of the compiler’s heart for the grasping of his son’s hand.
Having fashioned images resembling his new bride, he out of affection placed them within the bridal chamber of his house. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.70)
Then, with those ornaments brought by Dhaniṣṭhikā, as well as betel, sandalwood, new garments, and products of the nagas,
the Lord of Vraja [honored] her who was surrounded by her friends like a newlywed bride.
Having honored him, she became joyful, her heart overflowing with affection;
that which was taken by Rādhā at night was [returned] by Viśākhā. (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.71)
Dhaniṣṭhā gave a yellow upper garment secretly to Subala, and Subala also gave her a blue garment that had been taken from Kṛṣṇa by her very self.
Thus ends the second compendium, titled "The Compendium of the Morning Pastimes," within the *Śrī-Bhāvanā-sāra-saṅgraha* (Govinda-līlāmṛta 4.72).
